title: THE DAY YOU WILL NO LONGER NEED FAITH: What Paul Really Meant When He Said, “When the Perfect Comes, the Partial Will Pass Away”
paragraphs: THE DAY YOU WILL NO LONGER NEED FAITH: What Paul Really Meant When He Said, “When the Perfect Comes, the Partial Will Pass Away”

One of the most debated verses in the Bible contains a promise so breathtaking that it changes how we understand spiritual gifts, suffering, prophecy, love, and the day we finally see Jesus face to face. But have we been arguing about what will disappear while overlooking the One who will remain?
There is coming a day when you will never have to pray through tears again.
Not because prayer has failed.
But because the distance between what you believe and what you finally see will be gone.

There is coming a day when you will never have to ask God why He allowed something to happen. Never have to stare at a hospital ceiling wondering whether heaven heard your cries. Never have to open your Bible with trembling hands, desperately searching for one more promise to help you survive another night.

There is coming a day when the believer who has spent a lifetime saying, “Lord, I trust You, even though I do not understand,” will finally stand in the presence of the One who was faithful through every unanswered question.
And suddenly, the shadows will give way to sight.
But here is the question that has divided sincere, Bible-believing Christians for generations.
When Paul wrote, “But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Corinthians 13:10, KJV), what exactly was he talking about?
Was he predicting the completion of the New Testament?
Was he announcing the eventual disappearance of miraculous spiritual gifts?
Was he describing the maturity of the Church?
Or was he pointing toward something far greater—the day when God's redeemed people finally enter the fullness of His promised glory?
Before you decide, there is something you need to see.
Because one Greek word, one illustration about childhood, and one extraordinary promise about seeing “face to face” may completely change the way you read this passage.
And what makes this so important is that Paul was not writing to satisfy our curiosity about the future.
He was confronting a church that had spiritual gifts but was struggling to love.
A church that could speak impressively but could still wound people deeply.
A church that possessed genuine spiritual blessings but was tempted to confuse spiritual activity with spiritual maturity.
Does that sound uncomfortably familiar?
You can know the right verses and still speak cruelly to your family.
You can defend sound doctrine online and still destroy another believer with your words.
You can serve in ministry, give generously, teach Scripture, and become so occupied with proving that you are right that you forget what it means to love.
And Paul looks directly into that contradiction.
He does not begin by telling the Corinthians to become more impressive.
He tells them something far more devastating.
Without love, even extraordinary spiritual activity amounts to nothing.
“If I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2, ESV).
Read those final words again.
“I am nothing.”
Not merely less effective.
Not simply spiritually immature.
Nothing.

Paul was not saying truth is unimportant. He was not dismissing doctrine, spiritual gifts, or faithful service. He was exposing the terrifying possibility of possessing religious knowledge without displaying the character of Christ.
And that is where our investigation must begin.
Because if we tear 1 Corinthians 13:10 away from Paul's argument about love, we may win a theological debate while missing the very correction the Holy Spirit intended the Corinthians to receive.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 13:8–10:
“For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.
“But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away.” (KJV)
Now listen to the original Greek of verse 10:
ὅταν δὲ ἔλθῃ τὸ τέλειον, τὸ ἐκ μέρους καταργηθήσεται.
Hotan de elthē to teleion, to ek merous katargēthēsetai.
A careful translation is:
“But when the complete comes, what is partial will be brought to an end.”
The crucial expression is τὸ τέλειον (to teleion).
The adjective teleios can describe something mature, complete, fully developed, or having reached its intended goal. Its meaning depends on context.
And here is a detail that matters enormously.
Paul uses the neuter form, to teleion, meaning “the perfect” or “the complete.”
Some people argue that because the Greek expression is neuter, it cannot refer to Jesus Christ, who is a person.
But that argument goes too far.
The grammatical gender of an expression does not, by itself, settle what reality the expression describes. At the same time, Paul does not literally write, “When Jesus comes,” in verse 10.
We must not put words into the apostle's mouth, even when those words express a truth we cherish.
The real question is not whether teleion sounds spiritual enough to refer to Christ.
The question is what Paul means by the contrast between the partial and the complete.
And the next three verses are where the answer begins to emerge.
Paul continues:
“When I was a child, I spake as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child: but when I became a man, I put away childish things.
“For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
“And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.” (1 Corinthians 13:11–13, KJV)
Notice Paul's progression.
First, he contrasts childhood with adulthood.
Then, he contrasts an indirect, obscure view with seeing face to face.
Finally, he contrasts knowing in part with knowing in a fuller way.
These are not three unrelated thoughts.
They are illustrations explaining the difference between our present limitations and the fullness toward which God is leading His people.
The Greek expression for “in part” is ἐκ μέρους (ek merous).
It describes something partial rather than complete.
Paul is not saying that everything Christians presently know is false.
He is saying that what we know, even through God's genuine revelation, does not exhaust the fullness of what we will one day know.
Think about that.
The apostle Paul himself—the man who encountered the risen Christ, received extraordinary revelations, and wrote Scripture under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit—could still say:
“Now I know in part.”

If Paul could acknowledge the limits of his present understanding, perhaps we should be more careful about treating every theological disagreement as proof that everyone who disagrees with us is spiritually blind.
There are truths God has revealed clearly.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
He died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again on the third day.
Salvation is by God's grace through faith, not by human achievement.
And there are realities we understand truly but not exhaustively.
We can know God faithfully without claiming to comprehend everything about His eternal purposes.
We can trust His character without pretending to possess every answer.
We can hold biblical convictions firmly while acknowledging that sincere Christians have reached different conclusions about certain disputed passages.
That is not a surrender of truth.
It is humility before the God whose wisdom exceeds our own.
Now look at the phrase that may be the strongest clue in the entire passage.
“But then face to face.”
In Greek:
πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον (prosōpon pros prosōpon).
Literally, “face to face.”
Paul says that right now we see as though through a mirror, indirectly and obscurely.
The Greek phrase is δι’ ἐσόπτρου ἐν αἰνίγματι (di’ esoptrou en ainigmati).
It conveys seeing by means of a mirror, in an obscure or enigmatic way.
In Corinth, mirrors were generally made of polished metal rather than modern glass. They could reflect a recognizable image, but they did not provide the clarity of direct sight.
Paul's point is not that God's revelation is deceptive.
It is that our present perception is limited.
We truly see.
But we do not yet see as we one day will.
And Paul's language may recall Numbers 12:8, where God distinguishes His unusually direct communication with Moses from the visions and dreams given to other prophets.
In the Greek Old Testament, the language of speaking directly and not through riddles provides a striking background to Paul's contrast.
That connection is important because Paul is not merely discussing how much information believers possess.
He is describing a profound change in the manner and fullness of knowing.
Now we see indirectly.
Then, face to face.
Now we know partially.
Then, we will know more fully.
But what does that mean for the debate about “the perfect”?

One interpretation, commonly associated with cessationist theology, understands the perfect as the completion of the apostolic revelation preserved in the New Testament, or as the Church reaching a stage of maturity associated with that completed revelation.
According to this understanding, certain revelatory gifts served a foundational purpose during the apostolic era and ceased when that purpose was fulfilled.
Those who hold this position often emphasize the importance of the completed Scriptures and the unique foundational role of the apostles and prophets described in passages such as Ephesians 2:20.
Their concern is understandable.
The Church must never place alleged new revelations above, alongside, or in competition with the authoritative Word of God.
Scripture is God-breathed and equips believers for faithful service, as 2 Timothy 3:16–17 teaches.
We should take that conviction seriously.
But we must also ask whether the completion of the New Testament is what Paul specifically means in 1 Corinthians 13:10.
And here the interpretation encounters an important difficulty.
Paul does not explicitly mention the completed biblical canon.
Nor does he say, “When the final apostolic writings have been collected, then we shall see face to face.”
That does not automatically settle the larger debate about whether particular spiritual gifts continue today.
But it does mean we should be cautious about making this passage say more than its words establish.
The phrase “then shall I know even as also I am known” also seems to describe something far greater than possessing a complete collection of inspired writings.
Paul uses the Greek expression:
τότε δὲ ἐπιγνώσομαι καθὼς καὶ ἐπεγνώσθην.
Tote de epignōsomai kathōs kai epegnōsthēn.
A careful rendering is:
“Then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.”
The verb epiginōskō can convey recognition or fuller knowledge, depending on context.
Paul is not promising that redeemed human beings will become omniscient.
Only God possesses unlimited knowledge.
The comparison does not require that our future knowledge become infinite or equal to God's.
Rather, Paul anticipates a remarkable fullness of personal knowledge beyond the limitations of our present condition.
And that sounds deeply consistent with the hope of final redemption.
Consider what John writes:
Did you catch that?
“We shall see him as he is.”
Not merely hear about Him.
Not merely study descriptions of Him.
Not merely read the promises of His coming.
We shall see Him.
The One whose hands were pierced.
The One who carried our sins.
The One who conquered death.
The One who remained faithful when we were weak.

This is why many interpreters understand “the perfect” in 1 Corinthians 13:10 as the consummation of God's redemptive purposes at Christ's return, when believers enter the fullness of life promised in Him.
This interpretation takes seriously Paul's movement from partial knowledge to fuller knowledge, from indirect sight to face-to-face encounter, and from present limitations to future completeness.

It also resonates with 1 Corinthians 1:7–8, where Paul describes believers awaiting the revealing of Jesus Christ, and with 1 Corinthians 15, where he explains the resurrection and the final victory over death.
There is also an interpretation that emphasizes the Church's maturity rather than directly identifying the perfect with the final state.
Paul does use language related to maturity elsewhere, including in 1 Corinthians 14:20.
So that possibility deserves consideration.
Nevertheless, the sweeping contrast between present obscurity and future face-to-face knowledge makes the final consummation a particularly compelling reading of 1 Corinthians 13:10–12.
The strongest contextual reading is that Paul points beyond the present age toward the fullness of God's redemptive work, ultimately realized through Jesus Christ.
But we should distinguish that conclusion from a separate question.
Does this passage, by itself, prove that every miraculous or revelatory gift must continue unchanged until Christ returns?
No.
And does it, by itself, prove that all such gifts ceased when the New Testament was completed?
No.
Those broader questions require careful examination of additional biblical passages.
Faithful Christians disagree about them.
Some believe the New Testament teaches the cessation of certain gifts associated with the apostolic foundation.
Others believe the Spirit continues to distribute the gifts described in the New Testament, subject always to biblical testing and the authority of Scripture.
But whatever position we hold, Paul's central argument must not be lost.
Spiritual gifts are not the destination. Love is indispensable, and the fullness of God's promised future is still ahead of us.
And now the passage becomes painfully personal.
Because there is something deeply revealing about the fact that Paul places this discussion inside a chapter about love.
Imagine a man who can explain the Greek grammar of 1 Corinthians 13 with extraordinary precision.
He can debate cessationism and continuationism.
He can quote respected theologians.
He can identify interpretive weaknesses in competing positions.
He can defend his conclusions with confidence.
But when his wife tries to tell him that she is hurting, he refuses to listen.
When his child makes a mistake, he humiliates rather than restores.
When a struggling believer asks for help, he responds with contempt.
When someone challenges him, he becomes cruel.
He knows the language of spiritual maturity.
But he has forgotten the shape of Christian love.
And Paul's words confront him.
Not because sound doctrine is unnecessary.
But because truth that never shapes our conduct has not been allowed to accomplish its proper work in us.
Jesus did not say that His disciples would be recognized merely by their ability to win arguments.
He said:
“By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.” (John 13:35, KJV)
And before anyone mistakes this for a call to abandon conviction, remember that biblical love does not rejoice in unrighteousness.
It rejoices in the truth.
Love does not require us to affirm sin.
It requires us to speak truth without abandoning compassion, patience, and humility.
It calls us to confront wrongdoing when necessary, but never to confuse cruelty with courage.
Sometimes the most difficult evidence of spiritual maturity is not what you can explain from a pulpit.
It is how you respond when someone wounds your pride.
It is whether you can apologize without defending yourself.
It is whether you can forgive without pretending evil was harmless.
It is whether you can remain faithful when obedience costs you something.
And perhaps the hardest question is this:
What if the person who knows the most about spiritual gifts is not necessarily the person who most clearly reflects the character of the Savior?
Paul had already answered that question.
Love is patient.
Love is kind.
Love is not arrogant.
Love does not insist on its own way.
And love never ends.
The Greek words behind “love never ends” are:
Ἡ ἀγάπη οὐδέποτε πίπτει.
Hē agapē oudepote piptei.
Literally, “Love never falls” or “Love never fails.”
The word agapē here describes the love Paul has been explaining through its actions and character.
It is not merely emotional intensity.
It is love expressed through patience, kindness, truthfulness, endurance, and self-giving concern for others.
And Christians understand the deepest revelation of this love through Jesus Christ.
The cross is where we see that God's love is neither sentimental indulgence nor indifference toward evil.
Christ died for sinners.
Sin was not ignored.
Grace was not cheap.
Mercy was extended at immeasurable cost.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we learned enough theology to deserve His attention.
Not after we repaired every broken part of our lives.
Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
And that changes everything.
Because the Gospel does not tell us that we must become perfect before Jesus will receive us.
It tells us that Jesus Christ, the sinless Savior, gave Himself for sinners and rose again so that those who repent and trust in Him may be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed by His grace.
His finished work is the foundation of our salvation.
Our growing holiness is its fruit, not its purchase price.
The scandal of our sin is real.
But so is the astonishing grace of the Savior.
That is why our message remains:
Not because Jesus makes the consequences of every earthly decision disappear.
Not because following Him guarantees an easy life.
Not because every wound heals on our preferred schedule.
But because sin, shame, and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
Christ does.
And now return to Paul's words.
“When the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.”
Think of the Christian mother who has prayed for her wandering son for twenty years.
Think of the father who buried a child and still carries questions he cannot put into words.
Think of the believer who fights temptation in secret, falls, repents, gets up, and clings again to the mercy of Jesus.
Think of the exhausted servant of God who continues doing what is right even though nobody notices.
Think of the person reading this who has been quietly asking:
“Lord, when will I finally understand?”
Paul does not promise that every painful mystery will be explained to us in the precise way we imagine.
Scripture does not give us permission to invent those details.
But it does promise that our present experience of weakness, incompleteness, and limited sight is not the final condition of the redeemed.
Christ will return.
The dead in Christ will be raised.
Death will be defeated.
God will dwell with His people.
And Revelation 21:4 promises that He will wipe away every tear from their eyes.
No more death.
No more mourning.
No more crying.
No more pain.
Not because human history never mattered.
But because God will bring His redemptive purposes to their promised completion.
Imagine the difference between knowing that Jesus is faithful and finally beholding the Savior whose faithfulness carried you.
Imagine the difference between reading about the resurrection and standing in the reality of resurrection life.
Imagine the difference between praying, “Come, Lord Jesus,” and experiencing the fulfillment of that hope.
This is not escapism.
It is Christian hope anchored in the resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And this hope is meant to change how we live now.
If the fullness is still coming, then we must not pretend we have already arrived.
If our knowledge is still partial, we must resist spiritual arrogance.
If love endures beyond the temporary forms of our present ministry, we must not sacrifice love on the altar of appearing spiritually powerful.
If Christ is the fulfillment of our hope, then no spiritual gift, teacher, ministry, church tradition, or human personality should take His place.
Even the best ministry is temporary.
Even the most gifted preacher is limited.
Even the most carefully written article can only point beyond itself.
Jesus Christ is not merely a subject to be studied. He is the Lord to whom every faithful study of Scripture must lead.
And that brings us to one of the most misunderstood statements in this passage.
“And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity.”
Why is love the greatest?
Faith trusts God's promises.
Hope looks toward their fulfillment.
Love belongs to the very character of God and is essential to the life He calls His people to share.
Paul does not explain every detail of how faith and hope relate to the eternal state.
We should therefore be careful about claiming that 1 Corinthians 13:13, by itself, provides a complete timetable for their disappearance.
But the wider biblical hope is clear.
What we now await will one day be fulfilled.
Romans 8:24 reminds us that hope concerns what we do not yet see.
And 2 Corinthians 5:7 says:
“For we walk by faith, not by sight.”
Today, we walk by faith.
One day, the redeemed will behold Christ in the fullness of His revealed glory.
Today, we hope for the resurrection.
One day, the resurrection promise will be realized.
And throughout our present lives, love must remain central.
Not because love replaces the Gospel.
But because the Gospel reveals God's love and produces love in those transformed by His grace.
Now consider something that may challenge you more deeply than the theological debate itself.
What are you doing with the light God has already given you?
You may not understand every disputed passage.
You may not have resolved every question about spiritual gifts.
You may not know why God allowed certain chapters of your life to unfold as they did.
But you know enough to come to Jesus.
You know enough to repent of the sin you have been excusing.
You know enough to seek forgiveness from the person you wounded.
You know enough to stop using theological knowledge as a shield against personal obedience.
You know enough to open your hands and say:
“Lord, I do not understand everything. But I know I need You.”
And perhaps that is where real transformation begins.
Not when you finally win every argument.
But when the truth you defend begins to govern the way you live.
When your private life begins to reflect your public confession.
When your love for Christ becomes visible in your treatment of others.
When you stop demanding that God explain everything before you will obey what He has already made clear.
There is a reason this passage matters so much to Gospel Warrior.
We do not want to build a community that merely collects Bible information.
We want to help cultivate disciples who know Scripture, test what they hear, grow in discernment, repent sincerely, love deeply, and follow Jesus Christ faithfully.
A community where struggling believers can admit that they need prayer.
Where those wrestling with theological questions are encouraged to search the Scriptures carefully.
Where believers are strengthened without being taught to depend on a human ministry more than on Christ.
And where the Gospel remains more important than popularity, merchandise, algorithms, or the size of an audience.
These resources are offered to help believers grow deeper in Scripture, strengthen their faith, and become more rooted in Jesus Christ.
If this article helped you understand a difficult passage, consider saving it. Return to the Greek expressions, compare the verses, and examine the argument for yourself.
Do not simply accept an interpretation because it sounds powerful.
Be like the Bereans in Acts 17:11, who examined the Scriptures to see whether what they were hearing was true.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to prove that your side is superior.
But to invite a more careful, Christ-centered conversation.
And please do not leave this conversation without reflecting on the question beneath the debate.
Are you more concerned about proving what “the perfect” means, or about allowing the love of Christ to transform the imperfect parts of your life right now?
A community committed to biblical truth should never be afraid of careful questions.
We can pursue conviction without contempt.
We can disagree without dehumanizing.
We can correct one another without forgetting that we ourselves are still being sanctified.
For those who choose to give regularly as an expression of Christian generosity, that support can be part of their personal stewardship before God.
But we want to be biblically clear about something important.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and cheerful—not compelled by guilt or pressure.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.”
You glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, generosity, and faithful stewardship in the many places He has called you to serve.
Your local church, your family responsibilities, and the needs of those around you also deserve prayerful consideration.
Those products are not the heart of the mission.
Christ is.
No one needs to purchase access to the grace of God.
The Gospel is not for sale.
Jesus Christ is the Savior, and salvation is received by grace through faith in Him.
“When the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.”
For centuries, believers have debated what those words mean for prophecy, tongues, knowledge, and the future of spiritual gifts.
Those questions matter.
They deserve serious biblical study.
But imagine spending your entire life debating the meaning of perfection while refusing to surrender the bitterness in your own heart.
Imagine becoming an expert in the language of love while withholding love from the people God has placed beside you.
Imagine knowing the difference between teleios and ek merous but never allowing the truth of Christ's grace to soften your pride.
What a tragedy that would be.
Because the same Savior who promises a glorious future is calling us to repentance and faithful obedience today.
He is calling the proud to humility.
The bitter to forgiveness.
The wandering to return.
The exhausted to find their rest in Him.
The religious performer to stop hiding behind appearances.
The sinner to come to the cross.
And the believer who feels overwhelmed by unanswered questions to remember that partial sight is not the same as abandoned hope.
You may not understand everything today.
You may still be waiting for answers.
You may still be carrying scars that nobody else can see.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your present weakness is not the conclusion of your story.
Your hope rests not in your ability to understand every mystery, but in the crucified and risen Savior who will faithfully accomplish all that He has promised.
One day, faith will give way to sight in the fullness of God's appointed future.
One day, the shadows will be gone.
One day, the redeemed will behold the glory of the Lord.
And until that day, we are called to hold fast to His Word, walk humbly, love faithfully, and fix our eyes on Jesus.

The greatest tragedy would not be reaching the end of your life without understanding every mystery—it would be spending your life studying the promise of seeing Jesus while refusing to follow Him today.
